abstract: The Business Formation Statistics (BFS) program from the US Census Bureau provides timely, high-frequency data on new business applications and formations across the United States. The program tracks two primary application series: High-Business-Propensity Applications (HBA) and Corporation Business Applications (CBA), which serve as leading indicators of actual business formation. BFS publishes monthly and weekly data with seasonal adjustment, offering near-real-time visibility into entrepreneurial activity. The program is maintained through research partnerships with economists from the Federal Reserve Board, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, University of Maryland, and University of Notre Dame. As of January 2026, the program transitioned from 2017 NAICS to 2022 NAICS classification and began excluding internet sales applications from HBA and CBA metrics to better reflect likelihood of actual business formation. BFS data are essential for measuring whether AI-driven disruption is creating new entrepreneurial opportunities or suppressing business formation in exposed sectors.
keyFindings: BFS tracks both business applications (intent to form) and actual formations (firm births), enabling measurement of the application-to-formation conversion rate across sectors and time periods.

High-Business-Propensity Applications (HBA) and Corporation Business Applications (CBA) serve as leading indicators, with HBA designed to capture applications most likely to result in actual employer businesses.
The January 2026 methodological update excluded internet sales applications from headline metrics, representing a significant change in how digital-native business formation is measured.
Weekly and monthly publication frequency enables tracking of rapid shifts in entrepreneurial activity that may correlate with AI adoption waves or economic disruption events.
methodology: Administrative data program using IRS Employer Identification Number (EIN) applications as the primary source. Applications are classified by type (HBA, CBA) and mapped to NAICS sectors. Monthly and quarterly series are seasonally adjusted. Annual revisions incorporate Business Dynamic Statistics to validate formation counts against actual firm births.
qualifiers: BFS measures applications for EINs, not actual business success or survival. The 2022 NAICS transition and exclusion of internet sales applications create breaks in historical comparability. The program does not directly capture AI-related business formation or track technology adoption by new businesses. Solo proprietorships without employees may not require EINs and are thus undercounted.
